source_file: zhihu_CS专业留学生毕业之后留美的难度有多大.txt

heuristics.rule: Start LeetCode prep before arriving in the US — ideally 3 months before fall semester
heuristics.condition: When you are an international CS student planning to enter a US master's program in August...
heuristics.action: Begin grinding LeetCode from May, aiming to have a solid foundation before the September career fair season opens
heuristics.because: The best answer states that September career fairs begin immediately after August enrollment, leaving almost no time to prepare after arrival; the commenter notes that most students who fail had done fewer than 200 problems before interviewing

heuristics.rule: Apply to a minimum of 200 companies before concluding the job market is difficult
heuristics.condition: When an international CS student has not yet found a job offer...
heuristics.action: Continue applying until reaching at least 200 applications, not 20–30
heuristics.because: The best answer's author reports applying to 200+ companies with 100+ referrals and getting only 4–5 offers, citing the structural disadvantage of H-1B sponsorship scarcity as the reason volume is essential

heuristics.rule: Prioritize fall recruiting (September–December) over spring recruiting
heuristics.condition: When a first-year CS master's student is deciding when to focus recruiting energy...
heuristics.action: Treat September–December as the primary recruiting window and lock in a summer internship; treat January–March spring recruiting as a backup with significantly fewer spots
heuristics.because: The best answer explicitly states that spring recruiting has far fewer openings ('坑少了太多') and advises treating fall as the main — and strategically critical — window

heuristics.rule: Deliberately select easy coursework to free time for job preparation
heuristics.condition: When a CS master's student must balance coursework and recruiting...
heuristics.action: Choose easier electives, minimize GPA optimization effort, and redirect that time to LeetCode and applications
heuristics.because: The best answer argues that no employer asks about GPA after hiring, but every employer asks where you work — signaling that course performance has near-zero return compared to interview preparation

heuristics.rule: Maintain active communication with recruiters even after a head-count rejection
heuristics.condition: When a recruiter expresses interest but cannot extend an offer due to headcount constraints...
heuristics.action: Stay in contact and follow up in subsequent recruiting cycles
heuristics.because: Answer [1] describes how the UCLA student stayed in contact with LinkedIn HR after a headcount rejection and was later offered a fall internship directly without re-interviewing

heuristics.rule: If still struggling after two semesters, consider paying for a coding bootcamp or prep service rather than continuing to fail alone
heuristics.condition: When a student has completed two semesters of a CS master's and still cannot pass technical interviews...
heuristics.action: Invest in structured paid prep rather than continuing the same self-study approach
heuristics.because: The best answer frames this as having 'no retreat path' — failing the fall new-grad cycle means returning to China, so the cost of not improving exceeds the cost of a prep program

decision_factors.factor: LeetCode problem count and depth before first interview
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Both top answers independently identify insufficient LeetCode practice as the primary cause of interview failure — not visa status, school rank, or discrimination
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Count total problems solved with at least two full passes; the best answer suggests 500+ problems solved twice as a meaningful threshold for competitive companies

decision_factors.factor: Resume relevance to the role being targeted
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The best answer describes candidates submitting chemistry or EE content to CS roles, or listing irrelevant coursework — resulting in zero interview callbacks regardless of actual ability
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check whether every line item on the resume maps directly to the job description of the target role; anything unrelated should be removed

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Answer [2] argues that work experience dominates school prestige in US hiring — a candidate from a lower-ranked school with 3 years of experience outcompetes a fresh UIUC grad
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Evaluate whether the student has at least one US-based software engineering internship on their resume before applying for full-time roles

decision_factors.factor: Timing of application relative to recruiting cycle
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Answer [1] describes missing the entire fall recruiting cycle during the first semester due to late awareness — the student had no interviews while peers already had offers
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify whether the student understands the September career fair season and has begun applying by then; late starters face a structurally depleted opportunity set

decision_factors.factor: H-1B sponsorship availability at target companies
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The best answer notes that most US companies will not sponsor H-1B, making volume of applications necessary to find the subset that will
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research each company's historical H-1B sponsorship record before investing application effort; prioritize companies with confirmed sponsorship history

decision_factors.factor: Graduation timing relative to OPT start eligibility
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Answer [1] describes deliberately delaying graduation by two semesters to gain additional internship cycles under CPT, effectively creating more job-search runway
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate how many recruiting cycles remain before graduation and whether a strategic delay would add a meaningful internship or recruiting window

decision_factors.factor: Year of graduation relative to market saturation
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Answer [2] draws a sharp distinction between pre-2017 (trivially easy to find work) and post-2017 (requires genuine effort and some luck), and notes 2020 COVID impact as an additional compounding factor
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess current market conditions — PhD candidates were finding 100% intern placement while MS candidates were at roughly 50% in the post-2020 market described

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a high-prestige large company (e.g., LinkedIn, FAANG)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Internal team culture can be highly unpleasant even at brand-name firms — Answer [1] describes a LinkedIn team that functioned like a Chinese domestic company with high implicit pressure, causing the intern to want to quit by week 5
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who optimize purely for resume brand without researching team culture or who assume big-name companies have uniformly positive work environments

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Delaying graduation to get additional internship cycles
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Additional semesters require tuition payment unless a TA/RA full-funding arrangement is secured; the financial cost can be significant
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Self-funded students who delay graduation without securing a funded position — they pay tuition for extra semesters while also forgoing income

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Targeting only top-tier companies (Google, Facebook, etc.) from the start
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Students who fail to land FAANG may never have invested in the volume-based strategy that would have secured a smaller company offer, leaving them with no offer at all rather than a stepping-stone role
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students with moderate preparation who have an all-or-nothing FAANG mindset and skip the broader application funnel

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Enrolling in an ICC (Indian consulting company) placement service
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: ICC typically requires surrendering the first month's salary plus training fees; the financial cost is substantial even when the outcome (job placement) is successful
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students with weak backgrounds who use ICC as a last resort — they get placed but with a significant financial penalty and potential legal/immigration compliance risk not discussed in the posts

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Focusing intensely on GPA and academic performance during the master's program
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: High GPA does not translate to interview success or hiring outcomes — no employer asked about GPA after hiring, according to the best answer — while the time cost of GPA optimization comes directly at the expense of LeetCode and application volume
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students from academic backgrounds who default to the metrics that worked in school, especially those from Chinese undergraduate systems where GPA was decisive

failure_patterns.pattern: Interviewing at top companies (FAANG) after only 1–2 months of LeetCode preparation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students underestimate the preparation required because they see peers getting offers and assume the gap is small; optimism bias and social proof from occasional success stories distort the baseline
failure_patterns.consequence: Systematic rejection from target companies, followed by narrative attribution to visa discrimination or market difficulty rather than under-preparation
warning_signs: Student has solved fewer than 200 LeetCode problems before applying to Google/Facebook/Amazon
Student describes the job market as 'very difficult' after fewer than 50 applications

failure_patterns.pattern: Submitting irrelevant resumes — EE, chemistry, or non-CS content to CS software engineering roles
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students transitioning from other majors populate their resumes with the only experience they have, not recognizing that a hiring manager filters for role-relevant keywords before reading further
failure_patterns.consequence: Zero interview callbacks despite applying broadly; the student interprets this as market rejection rather than a resume targeting problem
warning_signs: Resume contains coursework or project descriptions from a different major
Student reports applying to CS roles but getting no responses at all

failure_patterns.pattern: Arriving at a US university in August with no prior job search preparation and expecting to find a role within the academic year
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students are focused on admissions and relocation; the job search feels like a post-arrival concern, not a pre-arrival priority
failure_patterns.consequence: Missing the September–December fall recruiting window entirely in the first year, forcing reliance on the spring cycle which has significantly fewer opportunities
warning_signs: Student has not started LeetCode before arriving in the US
Student has no draft resume when September career fairs begin

failure_patterns.pattern: Concluding the job market is inaccessible after applying to 20–30 companies
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students apply a domestic job-search mental model where 20–30 applications is a reasonable sample; they do not account for the structural H-1B sponsorship filter that reduces response rates for international candidates
failure_patterns.consequence: Premature abandonment of the job search, self-reinforcing belief that staying in the US is impossible, and potentially unnecessary return to home country
warning_signs: Student reports giving up after fewer than 50 applications
Student attributes failure to discrimination or luck without examining application volume

failure_patterns.pattern: Optimizing for coursework and GPA at the expense of recruiting activities
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students default to academic success metrics that rewarded them throughout their education; the incentive system in school does not reflect the incentive system in hiring
failure_patterns.consequence: Strong academic record but no job offer; GPA above 3.0 has near-zero marginal value in CS hiring while the time cost was enormous
warning_signs: Student spends more than 20 hours per week on coursework optimization during recruiting season
Student selects hard or prestigious courses when easier alternatives would free recruiting time

diagnostic_questions.question: How many LeetCode problems have you solved, and have you solved any of them twice?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student's preparation level is anywhere near competitive — the best answer suggests 500+ problems solved twice as a threshold; below 200 is identified as a near-certain failure condition for top companies
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is your breakdown across Easy/Medium/Hard, and are you solving unseen problems in under 30 minutes?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Stop applying to competitive companies immediately and return to preparation; your rejection rate will be near 100% and you are burning your recruiting window

diagnostic_questions.question: How many companies have you applied to so far?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student has invested sufficient volume to draw meaningful conclusions about their job search outcome; fewer than 100 applications is not a valid sample for an international student
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Of those, how many explicitly sponsor H-1B, and how many were applied to via referral versus cold application?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The student is likely drawing premature conclusions; the prescription is volume increase, not strategy change

diagnostic_questions.question: Does your resume contain only content directly relevant to the software engineering roles you are targeting?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the resume is filtering the student out before a human ever reads it; irrelevant content (EE projects, non-CS coursework) triggers instant rejection from CS roles
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are your projects and internships described in terms of technical impact and stack, or in terms of academic learning?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Resume revision is the first priority — no amount of application volume will work if the resume contains role-irrelevant content

diagnostic_questions.question: When did you start your job search preparation relative to your program start date?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student has already missed critical recruiting windows; students who start preparing after arriving in August have missed the ideal pre-arrival prep window and are competing against students who began months earlier
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you already applied to companies at the September career fair, and do you have any interviews scheduled?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The student needs to immediately assess which recruiting windows remain and create a compressed timeline to maximize remaining opportunities

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have any US-based internship experience on your resume before applying for full-time roles?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student is competing from a structurally weak position; Answer [2] argues that US work experience dominates school prestige in hiring decisions
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is the internship from a recognized US company, and can you speak technically and in depth about the work you did?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Consider whether delaying full-time applications to secure a first internship would strengthen the position, or whether the OPT timeline makes that infeasible

industry_realities.common_belief: CS job difficulty for international students is primarily caused by visa discrimination or market conditions beyond the student's control
industry_realities.actual_reality: The best answer argues — and Answer [2] partially corroborates — that the dominant cause of failure is insufficient preparation: under 200 LeetCode problems, weak resumes, and too few applications. The author states they have never personally seen a fully-prepared candidate (strong resume + 500+ problems + 200+ applications) fail to find a job
industry_realities.implication: Students who attribute failure to external factors without first auditing their preparation level are likely misdiagnosing their situation and therefore applying the wrong fix

industry_realities.common_belief: A high GPA from a good program is a meaningful signal that will help in the CS job search
industry_realities.actual_reality: Neither top answer mentions GPA as a meaningful factor in CS hiring outcomes. Answer [2] explicitly states that above 3.0 GPA has no marginal value; Answer [1] states that no employer asked about GPA after hiring. What matters is internship experience and technical interview performance
industry_realities.implication: Students should stop optimizing for GPA beyond a 3.0 floor and redirect that time to LeetCode practice and application volume

industry_realities.common_belief: Going to a target school (UCLA, top CS program) gives you a significant structural advantage in recruiting
industry_realities.actual_reality: Answer [1] from a UCLA CS graduate describes being scooped by a career fair conversation that succeeded not because of school brand but because of a spontaneous interpersonal interaction; the author also describes peers from lower-ranked schools succeeding. Answer [2] explicitly states a 3-year-experienced graduate from Oklahoma University would beat a fresh UIUC grad
industry_realities.implication: School brand matters far less than students assume once you are in the job search; work experience and interview readiness are the dominant variables

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD students and MS students have roughly similar odds of landing CS internships at major companies
industry_realities.actual_reality: Answer [2] reports that in the post-2020 market, PhD candidates had near 100% intern placement rates at large tech companies while MS candidates were at roughly 50%
industry_realities.implication: MS students should not benchmark their job search experience against PhD peers or assume similar timelines and success rates apply

industry_realities.common_belief: The difficulty of finding a CS job in the US has been roughly constant over the past decade
industry_realities.actual_reality: Both answers describe a sharp structural shift around 2017: before 2017, any CS graduate who could pass a basic online assessment could find a job; after 2017, market saturation from domestic and international supply increases meant genuine preparation was required. COVID in 2020 added another discontinuity
industry_realities.implication: Advice from graduates of pre-2017 cohorts about how easy it was to find a CS job does not apply to current students; the market is structurally different

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: After 20–30 rejections, concludes that the market is inaccessible and complains on forums about visa barriers
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats 200+ applications as the minimum viable sample before drawing any conclusions; attributes low interview conversion to resume quality or application targeting before blaming market conditions
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students who misdiagnose the cause stop doing the right things and start doing the wrong things (seeking workarounds) rather than increasing volume and improving preparation

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Believes 50–100 problems is sufficient to interview at competitive companies; applies after 1–2 months of preparation
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Targets 500+ problems solved at least twice before interviewing at top companies; uses unseen problem performance as a self-assessment signal rather than problem count alone
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students who under-prepare systematically fail technical screens and burn their recruiting windows before reaching adequate readiness

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Lists all academic and work experience regardless of relevance, assuming more content signals more value
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Strips the resume to only role-relevant content, even if that means a sparse resume early in the transition; understands that irrelevant content actively hurts rather than helps
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Irrelevant content causes immediate rejection at the screening stage, preventing interviews that preparation would otherwise qualify the candidate for

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Time allocation during the master's program
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treats the program as primarily academic and plans to job search after getting settled; selects interesting or prestigious courses
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treats the program as primarily a job-search platform and selects courses explicitly to minimize time cost; frames GPA optimization as a negative-expected-value activity above the 3.0 threshold
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students who invest heavily in coursework during recruiting season miss the September–December window and find themselves in a structurally weaker spring market

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes big-name companies (FAANG) are superior environments and that smaller companies are consolation prizes
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Understands that large companies offer brand value but limited growth and potentially toxic internal cultures; small companies offer faster skill development and easier future transitions to larger companies
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students who fixate on FAANG and reject smaller companies as fallbacks may end up with no offer at all, while those who accept stepping-stone roles build the experience base that makes subsequent FAANG applications much stronger

community_misconceptions.misconception: Finding a CS job in the US is very hard for international students regardless of preparation level
community_misconceptions.why_believed: High-volume complaint posts from unprepared students dominate forum discourse; survivors who prepared adequately post less frequently; visa complexity creates a plausible structural explanation for failure
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: The best answer states — and provides a personal track record to support — that a candidate with strong resume, 500+ LeetCode, and 200+ applications has a near-100% success rate; the difficulty narrative is driven primarily by the 90%+ who were insufficiently prepared
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students read the difficulty narrative and lower their effort expectations, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy; they under-prepare and under-apply, then confirm the narrative with their own failure

community_misconceptions.misconception: Spring recruiting (January–March) is a viable primary strategy if you miss fall
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Spring recruiting does exist and does produce some placements; students who arrive late or take time to prepare assume they can recover in spring
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: The best answer explicitly describes spring recruiting as having significantly fewer openings ('坑少了太多') and advises treating it only as a backup; fall is the primary window with the overwhelming majority of CS headcount
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students who intentionally defer to spring or fail to prepare for fall find themselves competing for a fraction of available positions with the same or larger candidate pool

community_misconceptions.misconception: GPA matters significantly in CS job applications
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Academic success was the primary sorting mechanism throughout Chinese education; students naturally extend this model to the job market
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Above 3.0, GPA has negligible impact on CS hiring outcomes according to both answers; what matters is internship experience, LeetCode performance, and resume relevance
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students spend hundreds of hours optimizing GPA at the direct expense of LeetCode preparation and job applications — exactly the wrong tradeoff during a constrained recruiting window

community_misconceptions.misconception: Attending a top CS program (UCLA, UIUC, etc.) substantially improves your odds in CS job searches
community_misconceptions.why_believed: School prestige was a strong signal in admissions and in domestic Chinese hiring; the investment thesis of paying for a top program implicitly assumes prestige transfers to job outcomes
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Answer [2] explicitly argues that work experience dominates school prestige — a candidate from a lower-ranked school with relevant experience beats a fresh top-school graduate; Answer [1] confirms that UCLA brand did not prevent the author from struggling through two full recruiting cycles
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students over-invest in admissions prestige and under-invest in the preparation activities that actually drive hiring outcomes

community_misconceptions.misconception: ICC (Indian consulting companies) are scams or borderline illegal operations that should be avoided
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The fee structure (first month's salary surrender plus training fees) sounds exploitative; community posts often warn about ICC without distinguishing legitimate from fraudulent operators
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Answer [2] describes a specific case where a friend signed with an ICC, paid the fees, and successfully obtained a full-time Oracle role — concluding 'completely worth it'; the author notes ICC themselves have become selective and now screen applicants
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students who categorically reject ICC as an option may foreclose a viable path when their independent job search has failed; the legitimate tradeoff is financial cost versus access to a placement network

real_case_outcomes.situation: UCLA CS master's student from EE background, arrived with near-zero CS/LeetCode preparation, missed fall recruiting cycle entirely in first semester
real_case_outcomes.decision: Pursued a China-based internship (JD.com) in summer after Year 1 when no US internship was found; used subsequent semesters strategically to pursue two more US internships via CPT while deliberately delaying graduation
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Secured full-time offer at Credit Karma after LinkedIn fall internship; total program took three years instead of standard two; all classmates who wanted to stay in the US eventually found roles
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Recovery from a slow start is possible through strategic program extension and iterative internship accumulation, but the financial and time cost is significant; the earliest possible preparation still dominates

real_case_outcomes.situation: CS master's student reached out to a company recruiter at a career fair in an informal, non-pitch manner (commenting on the recruiter's reversed name badge)
real_case_outcomes.decision: Gave resume casually and walked away; later discovered this was the only company from that career fair to follow up
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Received interview, passed, and secured a summer internship at Symantec — later learned the recruiter deliberately screened for candidates who would speak up rather than passively network
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Authentic interpersonal interaction at career fairs can outperform polished pitching; some recruiters actively screen for personality traits (assertiveness, willingness to speak up) rather than technical credentials at the initial screening stage

real_case_outcomes.situation: Student received interest from LinkedIn during fall recruiting but was rejected due to headcount constraints
real_case_outcomes.decision: Maintained ongoing contact with the LinkedIn HR recruiter over several months
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Was offered a fall internship position directly, bypassing the interview process entirely, because the earlier interview performance was on record
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Headcount rejections are not permanent rejections; maintaining recruiter relationships after a near-miss can convert a timing failure into a deferred offer with no additional interviewing required

real_case_outcomes.situation: Student secured a LinkedIn internship (FAANG-equivalent prestige) only to find the team culture highly unpleasant — implicit pressure, all-Chinese team dynamic, weekend-boundary violations
real_case_outcomes.decision: Completed the internship while simultaneously interviewing at other companies; declined the return offer and joined a lower-prestige company with better culture fit
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Successfully transitioned to Credit Karma; describes the decision as correct in retrospect and the LinkedIn experience as a useful correction of prestige bias
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Prestige of employer does not predict quality of work experience; team culture varies enormously within large companies and can only be evaluated through direct experience; optimizing for brand at the expense of environment fit is a predictable source of regret

psychological_barriers.trigger: Student asks 'how hard is it to stay in the US with a CS degree?' in a way that seeks validation rather than information
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Catastrophizing and loss aversion — the student is framing the question to prepare emotionally for failure rather than to identify what actions would change the outcome
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Passive information-seeking on forums rather than active preparation; reading difficulty narratives as confirmation that external factors (visa, discrimination, market) are the binding constraint
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Redirect from the difficulty question to a preparation audit: 'How many problems have you solved? How many companies have you applied to? What does your resume look like?' — converting an emotional question into a diagnostic one

psychological_barriers.trigger: Student reports that they applied to 20–30 companies with no success and is now considering giving up or returning to China
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Availability bias — the student has a salient, painful recent experience (rejections) that is cognitively dominating their estimate of the overall probability
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Premature conclusion from an unrepresentative sample; framing of the situation as 'I tried and it didn't work' rather than 'I tried an insufficient amount'
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Provide the base rate: the best answer describes applying to 600+ companies as the high-effort benchmark; reframe 20–30 as not yet a job search, but the beginning of one

psychological_barriers.trigger: Student expresses shame about considering a paid prep service (bootcamp or ICC) after failing to find a job independently
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Identity threat — the student perceives needing external help as evidence of personal inadequacy rather than as a rational resource allocation decision
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Delayed decision to seek help until too late in the OPT window; continuing to attempt independent preparation that has already demonstrated insufficient results
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Normalize paid prep explicitly: 'There's nothing shameful about it' (直接原文: '没啥可耻的'); frame it as a return-on-investment calculation — the cost of a prep program is recoverable in weeks of US tech salary, while the cost of returning to China without a job is not

psychological_barriers.trigger: Student describes working at a prestigious company (FAANG) as a goal they pursued for years, then discovers the reality is disappointing
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Idealization and surrogate goal substitution — the student conflated 'working at Google/LinkedIn' (an observable, socially validated milestone) with 'having a good work life' (the actual goal)
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Shock and demoralization upon experiencing the gap between company brand and actual team environment; difficulty making the rational decision to leave because of sunk cost in the goal pursuit
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe prestige as a means, not an end: the informed pattern is to use large-company experience as a resume credential while actively evaluating whether the specific team is a good fit, and to leave without guilt when it is not

psychological_barriers.trigger: Student from a non-CS background (EE, chemistry) asks whether it is too late to transition into CS
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Temporal anxiety and comparison paralysis — the student is measuring their current state against CS-native peers and interpreting the gap as permanent rather than as a preparation problem
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Asking permission-seeking questions ('can I still make it?') rather than action-oriented ones ('what do I need to do?')
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Provide a concrete, unconditional answer (Answer [1] FAQ section: 'You can, as long as you want it and are willing to do the work') paired with a specific first action — start LeetCode, revise the resume to remove irrelevant content, find one CS project to add

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'How hard is it for CS international students to stay in the US after graduation?' — framed as a fixed external difficulty question
reframing_moves.reframe: The best answer reframes it as: 'The difficulty level is almost entirely determined by your preparation level — the people saying it's hard are overwhelmingly the people who didn't prepare'
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Converts a passive assessment of external conditions into an actionable internal audit; shifts locus of control from market/visa to preparation behavior
reframing_moves.example_language: 如果一个人CS背景+简历+刷题+投公司，每个都做了，说实话我没见过留不下来的 (If someone has done all four — CS background, resume, LeetCode, applications — honestly I've never seen anyone who couldn't stay)

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'I applied to companies and got rejected — the job market is too difficult for international students'
reframing_moves.reframe: The best answer reframes it as: 'You haven't applied enough to have a valid data point — 20 applications is not a job search for an international student, it's a warm-up'
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Removes the false sense of having genuinely tried by replacing it with a concrete, quantified benchmark (200+ applications); prevents premature attribution of failure to external causes
reframing_moves.example_language: 北美投简历，少于200家都是没努力 (In North America, applying to fewer than 200 companies means you haven't tried)

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'Should I focus on my coursework and GPA, or on finding a job?'
reframing_moves.reframe: The best answer reframes it as a false tradeoff with a clear answer: 'Nobody will ever ask your GPA; everyone will ask where you work — this is not a difficult optimization'
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Collapses what feels like a genuine dilemma into a decision with a dominant option; removes the cognitive burden of balance-seeking by making the asymmetry of payoffs explicit
reframing_moves.example_language: 毕业了没人问你GPA多少，都会问你去哪工作了，所以分清孰轻孰重 (After graduation no one asks your GPA, everyone asks where you work — understand what matters more)

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'Big companies are the goal; small companies are a fallback I'd rather avoid'
reframing_moves.reframe: Answer [2] reframes small companies as a different game with different advantages — better skill development, more responsibility, and a proven on-ramp to large companies with experience
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Reframes the hierarchy from a prestige ranking into a strategic choice with genuine tradeoffs; removes the stigma of small companies and converts them from consolation prizes into legitimate starting positions
reframing_moves.example_language: 在美国，有工作经验就是爸爸 (In America, having work experience makes you the boss — experience trumps school prestige)

_extraction_key: zhihu_zhihu_CS专业留学生毕业之后留美的难度有多大
